fullText:
Historically a new Grand Theft Auto game inspired controversy around violence – but this time people are getting exercised about its romance

There was never any doubt that Grand Theft Auto VI’s extended look would elicit a viral reaction from the internet. Having won the Game Awards’ Most Anticipated award twice consecutively, Rockstar’s forthcoming crime opus is one of the most frothed-over games in recent memory, or indeed ever. It’s nothing short of a cultural phenomenon.

One aspect of the game has provoked an unexpectedly vehement response on social media: not violence, but romance. Protagonists Lucia and Jason are in love, you see, and as a player, part of your job is keeping their spark alive and their relationship strong, so that their criminal escapades are underpinned by a strong connection to one another. Holding hands, enjoying a date at the beach, spontaneously texting one another when apart – all of these interactions will strengthen their bond. You’ll be putting in a lot of work to ensure this couple thrives, which is why some people have come to believe that playing GTA VI counts as micro-cheating.

Takes on this are all over social media. Multiple users have shared posts claiming that if you romance characters in video games such as GTA VI you’ve been unfaithful to your partner; TikTok account El Michelle remarked that simply playing the game is cheating. “In absolutely no human way is my fiance playing GTA VI,” posted Shelby Haas, another TikTok user. “You literally have to maintain a relationship with a girl […] you have to take her on dates, and you can have sex with her. […] Don’t let your boyfriend or fiance or husband play GTA 6.”

Over on TikTok, a post by Landry states that GTA VI “is basically the same as cheating”, continuing: “I guarantee you, if your man is playing GTA VI and keeping his little girlfriend alive on that video game, he’s most definitely the type that’s following models.”

GTA VI is by no means the inventor of in-game dating – hello, Baldur’s Gate 3, in which you can romance and have sex with any (or several) of your eight companions, including a druid who transforms into a bear. And surely we all remember trying to persuade our Sims to get off with each other. For at least 20 years dating and romance have been a significant element of all sorts of different titles; there is an entire (immensely popular) genre of dating games devoted to playfully living out virtual relationships.

Even so, due to its unrivalled online presence, GTA VI will be many people’s first exposure to the idea. Video game newcomers on TikTok seem especially exercised about the lengths their partners will go to to maintain a happy in-game relationship with Lucia, though it’s worth pointing out that it goes both ways: playing as Lucia, you’ll have to put just as much effort into maintaining a strong relationship with Jason. (The notion of maxing out the romance with Jason hasn’t provoked nearly as intense a response.)

It’s easy for people to revert to off-the-shelf misogynistic accusations about “jealous” and “overreactive” spouses in a situation like this, and indeed, many counter-commentators have done just that. “‘GTA VI is literally cheating’ is something I would say if I was a jealous, insecure hag […]” declares one TikToker. In the comments on one Instagram video, someone opined that GTA VI “promotes lust”, resulting in a massive pile-on.

But what if this isn’t knee-jerk jealousy? Behind these rather laughable concerns about virtual girlfriends, there are valid insecurities here over the idea of one’s real-life partner being more invested in a fictional character than a real-life relationship. Especially for young people, we’re in an age of loneliness and disconnection, fuelled by being chronically online. It’s one of the greatest paradoxes of modern society: despite being able to instantly engage with anyone or anything, these interactions are superficial and fleeting.

The dating scene right now is bleak. Dating columnist-cum-novelist Annie Lord believes the way we treat each other is part of the problem: “People treat each other as disposable because they’ve got the mindset of an app.” Factor in the growing influence of the manosphere, which many say has “ruined dating”, and it’s not hard to comprehend why experts say we’re experiencing a global dating crisis. Since 2014, the number of young people without close friendships/relationships has “risen fivefold”. Joke all you want about oversensitive gen Zs, but they are experiencing life in a social vacuum.

If you’re dealing in real life with men who don’t even text you back, let alone take you on a date, it’s easy to see why it would sting to watch them engage enthusiastically in a video-game relationship with a virtual woman whom they shower with expensive gifts, bouquets, and thoughtful messages. As TikToker RawTJR’s post joked: this is “how mfs gonna be treating Lucia in GTA 6 while treating their irl gf like shi”.

“I will NOT stand for people calling these partners ‘jealous’ or ‘overreacting’ when they clearly are trying to voice real concerns about their relationships,” wrote trans activist and sex educator Dee Whitnell in an Instagram post. “If someone feels underappreciated in their relationship but sees their partner fulfilling these needs for someone else (even if it is a game character), it’s totally understandable why they would feel a bit frustrated.”

As someone who explores every romance option in all games that allow it, I personally think it’s absurd to class in-game romances as a form of cheating – though I appreciate that individual boundaries can differ. People might more reasonably channel their concerns into conversations around AI companionship sites, such as Candy AI and DreamGF, that offer virtual sexbots. As far back as 2023 we were asking if an AI chatbot could be classed as cheating – and the technology has vastly improved since then.

More than anything else, this unexpected controversy around GTA VI highlights how dissatisfied and lonely many people are within their relationships. And a video game isn’t going to change that one way or another.

title: Former Colorado crime analyst gets 10-year prison sentence for manipulating DNA data
description: A judge sentenced a former forensic analyst for the Colorado Bureau of Investigation to 10 years in prison on Tuesday after authorities said her manipulation of DNA data raised questions about the val...
fullText:
GOLDEN, Colo. (AP) — A judge sentenced a former forensic analyst for the Colorado Bureau of Investigation to 10 years in prison on Tuesday after authorities said her manipulation of DNA data raised questions about the validity of hundreds of criminal cases.

Yvonne "Missy" Woods pleaded guilty in June to perjury, attempting to influence a public servant, forgery and committing a cybercrime. Dozens of other counts were dismissed as part of a plea agreement.

Problems with the scientist's work were found in cases involving homicide, sexual assault, robbery and other crimes, according to authorities. Prosecutors were forced to review hundreds of cases, and at least one murder conviction was vacated as a result of Woods' misconduct.

Woods had faced between 8 and 16 years in prison during Tuesday's sentencing hearing before state District Judge Andrew Poland in Golden, Colorado.

She resigned in 2023 after a decades-long career. Authorities accused her of altering data to conceal tampering, deleting data that showed she failed to troubleshoot issues within the testing process and not thoroughly documenting tests performed in case records.

Woods apologized during Tuesday's hearing but said she knew saying sorry would not undo the harm she caused, the Denver Post reported.

"For many years I was entrusted with evidence that could have profound consequences for defendants, victims, families and the courts. I failed that responsibility. I am deeply sorry for that failure," she said.

Following the sentencing, Colorado Bureau of Investigation officials said they have sought to reform their laboratories in response to the data scandal as they try to rebuild public trust.

"The actions of one individual never define this organization, and they do not define the dedicated public servants who continued showing up every day with integrity," bureau Director Armando Saldate said in a statement.

The investigation into Woods' misconduct began in September 2023 after an intern at the bureau discovered missing information in a case that Woods handled in 2018. According to an arrest affidavit, Woods allegedly told investigators at one point that she had changed data to complete cases more quickly.

In the vacated murder case, Michael Clark was released from prison in 2025 after his lawyers argued that DNA evidence was mishandled by Woods. Prosecutors said they would seek to retry him.

In two homicide cases, the defendants received lesser sentences under plea deals than they could have faced if they went to trial because prosecutors were afraid Woods' involvement could lead to acquittals.

Convictions in other cases also have been challenged in courts across Colorado.

A Colorado Bureau of Investigation internal affairs report in 2024 revealed that concerns about Woods' work first surfaced more than a decade ago. As early as 2014, a worker questioned her testing of evidence, and in 2018 she was temporarily removed from working on DNA cases after being accused of data manipulation, the report said.

State officials have said that the response to Woods' actions could end up costing more than $11 million.

title: Unearthed interview exposes what Talarico thought about 'tough-on-crime' tactics
description: Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico pushed restorative justice over suspension and expulsion, linking school discipline to criminal reform.
fullText:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate in Texas, once framed disciplinary practices in schools as an outflow of the ideas behind criminal justice reforms he hoped lawmakers would implement in Texas.

"I'm recently excited about the formation of a bipartisan criminal justice reform caucus in the Texas House with prominent Democrats and prominent Republicans who understand that we have to move away from a tough-on-crime approach to a smart-on-crime approach, and that, I think, filters down to our schools," Talarico said in a 2020 interview on school disciplinary practices and their effect on minorities.

Talarico's train of thought, from criminal reform laws to changes in educational discipline, demonstrates his underlying beliefs about moving away from punitive corrections.

Soros Network Rebuilds Progressive Prosecutor Push After String Of Election Losses

Talarico fleshed out his view, detailing how the changes would affect the educational system.

"[We are] starting in elementary school, where we really pursue restorative practices that are going to rehabilitate our students who are suffering from trauma, our students who are feeling unsafe in school and our students who harm a classroom community."

Talarico was referring to "restorative justice," a view that links misbehavior to past personal and emotional experiences. In the words of Texas Appleseed, a group that promotes "social, economic and racial justice," restorative justice in education emphasizes the relational cost of conflict as a way to deter future bad behavior. "Restorative Justice, when applied to a school setting, focuses on how student behavior has harmed others and how to make amends. Schools use it to build community and strengthen student–school connections," the group wrote in a definition submitted to lawmakers.

The approach is often mentioned as an alternative to "zero tolerance" policies that focus on punishments that deter discouraged conduct.

To Talarico, its adoption could deemphasize other forms of punishments.

"What that means is really allowing students to repair the harms that they've caused in a classroom community. It's a lot more rigorous and a lot more effective than just expelling a student or suspending a student or removing them from a classroom community," Talarico said.

While in the Texas legislature in 2021, Talarico introduced a bill, HB 62, which would have sought to move schools away from in-school suspension, out-of-school suspension and removing kids to alternative educational programs.

The bill stalled in committee and never became law.

North Carolina Teacher's Killing Reignites Scrutiny Of Roy Cooper's Criminal Justice Record In Senate Race

In the wake of the Uvalde school shooting in 2022, Republican lawmakers pushed back against Talarico's line of reasoning, arguing that, despite some calls for leniency, repercussions for problematic behavior are sometimes unavoidable.

"Look, I don't want to see a kid go to jail for being caught with some pot. I don't want to see a kid go to jail because he gets into a fight with another kid," Texas state Rep. Steve Toth, a Republican, told interviewers.

"That's clearly not the intent here. But if you've got a kid that is violent and is consistently violent, and they've been violent toward other children and teachers, then we either have to reach that kid or we have to remove that kid. They shouldn't be in the classroom. Period."

Talarico's statements are consistent with past calls to step away from law enforcement and prisons and towards social programs — calls that also show his beliefs about the best ways to deter criminal behavior.

"If we took just half of what we spent on wars, prisons, and policing and spent it on education, health care, and jobs, we could make prisons obsolete," Talarico said in a 2022 speech to a graduation ceremony for incarcerated students.

A little later on in that same speech, Talarico went further, calling the idea of prisons themselves a kind of violence.

"My experience as a teacher, a legislator, and a Christian tells me that birds don't belong in cages; children don't belong in cages; people don't belong in cages. Poverty is violence. Pollution is violence. And yes, prison is violence," Talarico said.

Michigan Senate Hopeful Abdul El-sayed Fires Back At Cnn Choosing To 'Fixate' On 'Defund The Police' Comments

"I'm not asking you to join the system; I'm asking you to change the system. Dismantle this system of violence."

When asked about his views on criminal justice and how they link to education, Talarico's campaign said he has always prioritized both safety and smart-on-crime approaches, noting that he had been a member of the state's criminal reform caucus.

"James joined his Republican colleagues on this caucus because as a former public school teacher, James cares about keeping Texas students safe. James agrees with most Texans that we government should be smart-on-crime, and our students deserve all the support possible," JT Ennis, a campaign spokesperson, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"While James has passed bills in the legislature to deny bail for violent criminals, crack down on violent felons and send billions of dollars to support law enforcement, Ken Paxton has abused his office to benefit his wealthy donors and the well-connected — allowing criminals back on the street even as it made Texans less safe. Even Ken Paxton's fellow Republicans have blasted his public safety record: more murders, soft on human trafficking, and pedophiles walking free," he added, referring to Talarico's Republican challenger, former Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton.

Having cleared the primary and secured his party's nomination, Talarico will face off against Paxton in the Nov. 3 general election.

Original article

title: Russia to strip contract soldiers of one-off payment if laws violated at home
description: Sept 8 () - Russia's defence ministry wants to claim back part of a one-off payout from contract service personnel ‌found guilty of criminal offences at home, a document ‌showed, amid increasing cases...
fullText:
Sept 8 (Reuters) - Russia's defence ministry wants to claim back part of a one-off payout from contract service personnel ‌found guilty of criminal offences at home, a document ‌showed, amid increasing cases of domestic violence among those fighting Russia's war on Ukraine.

Russia ​provides a minimum one-off payment of 400,000 roubles ($4,640) for soldiers signing at least a one-year contract to fight in the war with Ukraine that Moscow calls "a special military operation". Russia invaded Ukraine in February ‌2022.

In practice, one-off payouts ⁠may reach a few million roubles per soldier, depending on the region, in addition to a monthly ⁠salary. Russia is also reducing sentences for those serving time in prison in exchange for signing up for the war, among other benefits, as it ​seeks to ​bolster army numbers.

Russia has seen ​a rise in domestic violence ‌as fighters return home for leave, and the defence ministry wants to claim part of the one-off payments "in order to increase the motivation of military personnel to comply with the law", in case of a criminal offence, a draft law published on Monday showed.

If ‌active contract service members are found guilty of ​a criminal offence which does not imply ​a prison sentence, they ​should pay back a portion of the one-off ‌payout based on the months of ​the service left, ​the document showed.

Russia does not disclose official statistics on domestic violence committed by its service personnel but independent media, citing ​military courts data, ‌reported hundreds of such cases, including murders, since the start ​of the 2022 invasion.

title: Red Star fans unveil tifo of war criminal Mladic before derby
description: Red Star Belgrade fans unveil a tifo of war criminal Ratko Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade on Sunday.
fullText:
Red Star Belgrade fans unveiled a tifo of war criminal Ratko Mladic before their derby win over Partizan Belgrade on Sunday night.

Mladic, who died in a United Nations prison in August, was given a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity in 2017.

He and his troops were responsible for the systematic killing of the non-Serb population of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the wars in the former Yugoslavia between 1992 and 1995.

He oversaw the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica and a siege of the capital Sarajevo in which more than 10,000 people died.

Red Star have already been fined 90,000 euros (£77,000) this season by Uefa, external after their fans unveiled a banner commemorating Mladic in a Europa League play-off against Czech side FC Viktoria Plzen last month.

Red Star's social media accounts published a video of the tifo and the two teams observing a minute's silence for Mladic, alongside a saluting emoji.

The official X account of Bosnia-Herzegovina's national team replied with an obscenity.

After initially enjoying the protection of Serb president Slobodan Milosevic, who would later die while on trial for genocide himself, Mladic spent more than a decade on the run, eventually being found hiding out in a remote farmhouse.

However, he remains a celebrated figure for some in Serbia with thousands gathering at a church in Belgrade for his funeral on Monday.

title: Thousands gather in Belgrade for funeral of convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic
description: BELGRADE, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Thousands of people gathered in front of a church in Belgrade to pay respects to former Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic who died last week while serving a life sentence
fullText:
BELGRADE, Sept 7 (Reuters) - Thousands of people gathered in front of a church in Belgrade to pay respects to former Bosnian Serb General Ratko Mladic who died last week while serving a life sentence ‌for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Mladic remains a revered figure among many Serbs in ‌Serbia and in Bosnia's autonomous Serb Republic, despite his convictions linked to his role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre and in the siege of Sarajevo.

People ​carrying Serbian flags and pictures of Mladic wearing a traditional Serbian military cap arrived in front of the church to light candles early on Monday, hours before his scheduled burial.

Free bus services were offered from Bosnia and most towns in Serbia for anyone who wanted to pay their respects.

Mladic's coffin was displayed inside the church and six men, mainly war veterans ‌from Serbia and Bosnia, took turns guarding ⁠it. Mladic's wife, son, and grandchildren stood inside receiving condolences.

"Time will tell, time is the best judge who will show what kind of person is who and to whom," said ⁠Belgrade resident Jovan Vincic, who had come to the church.

CONFLICTS TRIGGERED BY BREAK-UP OF YUGOSLAVIA

Mladic's death has stirred up strong feelings linking back to the break-up of Yugoslavia and the ethnic conflicts that ensued in the Balkans.

Mladic was found guilty by the United ​Nations ​International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia of genocide for his ​role in the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, in which ‌about 8,000 Bosniak Muslim men and boys were killed after Bosnian Serb forces overran the U.N.-designated enclave.

He was also convicted over the 43-month siege of Sarajevo, during which about 10,000 people were killed.

Last week, EU enlargement commissioner Marta Kos postponed her visit to Serbia because of what she said was the "glorification" of Mladic after his death, including the use of a government plane to return him to Serbia.

Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic dismissed those statements, but did not ‌say whether he would attend Monday's funeral.

The service was scheduled to ​be conducted by the Patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox church at noon, after ​which Mladic will be buried in a nearby cemetery ​beside his daughter, who died in 1994.

In Sarajevo, meanwhile, the funeral rekindled painful memories of ‌the war.

"It is really horrible that this is taking ​place there (in Belgrade) because I ​know there are normal people who are against it," said Zdravka Gvozdjar, a retired pharmacist whose 9-year-old son was killed during the Sarajevo siege by a grenade fired by the Mladic-led forces, one among more ​than 1,000 children killed in the ‌city.

"Mladic ... only deserved to be erased from memory for good, not to be ... promoted as a hero," ​she said. "He should be remembered only as a butcher."

title: TV presenter among 11 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case
description: Sarah Khalifa is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues.
fullText:
Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges.

According to state-owned al-Akhram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them.

They also had illegal firearms and munitions.

Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges.

The verdict - which can be appealed against - was first announced last month.

However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases.

During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them.

Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Akhram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips.

According to the state-run Akhbar al-Youm newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices.

According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of whom were executed.

The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.

title: 'Naive' police staff who leaked information jailed
description: Two police call handlers have passed on information to their criminal boyfriends, a court heard.
fullText:
Two police call handlers who "flaunted" their training by looking up and passing on confidential information to criminals have been jailed.

Jessica Fitzhugh and Ellie-Mae Doherty, both 22, accessed personal details about their criminal boyfriends while working for Derbyshire Constabulary.

Fitzhugh, from Belper, admitted unauthorised access to computer material, and Doherty, from Ripley, pleaded guilty to the more serious offence of misconduct in a public office, after she passed on to her partner some of the information she found.

Doherty was jailed for 11 months and Fitzhugh for four months after a two-day hearing at Leicester Crown Court, which concluded on Thursday.

Following the investigation, the IOPC sent evidence to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) and the charges were authorised on 23 March.

Derbyshire Police said both Doherty and Fitzhugh "have left the organisation" and a misconduct hearing would now take place.

Temporary Deputy Chief Constable Michelle Shooter said: "[They] breached the trust and have faced the consequences of their actions."

In sentencing, Judge Timothy Spencer KC called them "naive", describing them as "girlfriends of two undesirable young men".

He said: "Regrettably and for reasons that now you will find impossible to rationalise, you both flaunted the clear training, the clear direction and the clear guidelines you were given by the Derbyshire Police.

"In your case, Ellie-Mae Doherty, it went further because the information you accessed was clearly passed on in two distinct ways at two distinct times."

Fitzhugh started working for the force in January 2023, when she was 19 years old, as a call handler and then a dispatcher, before referring her friend Doherty for a job, who joined as a call handler in September 2023, the court heard.

Both women went through "intense" vetting and were required to read and sign declarations stating that they had no contacts who were "engaged in criminal activities", the court heard.

Prosecuting, Helen Rodger said each had a sexual relationship with men involved in crime, and should have known that these were "disclosable associations".

The first time Doherty accessed information about an incident and passed it on to Robbie Braddock, with whom she was said to be in a relationship, was in December 2023, roughly two months after she completed her control room training.

Doherty shared details about the incident, a fight in which another male had smashed a window, with Braddock.

Rodger said a second incident involving Doherty on 6 March 2024, saw her access details about a search warrant being executed and pass on details about it to the same man as before.

Doherty viewed the details of the incident several times before also checking who was in custody at Ripley custody suite.

Fitzhugh, who was also said to be in a relationship with a man with a criminal record, looked up incidents in spring 2024, out of what the judge called "idle curiosity".

The two women, who met while both working at McDonald's before starting with the force, sat apart in the dock and were accompanied in court by their families.

Spencer speculated that maybe their "friendship has not survived this case" and said "I have little doubt that it will haunt you for the rest of your days".

He said: "It's impossible to recognise the young women who I read about, with such positive qualities, in the women who committed these offences."

Defending Fitzhugh, Elizabeth Power said she had a "lack of awareness" about the "severity of the breaches that she made".

Lowri Butterworth, for Doherty, told the court that she was "acutely aware" and had been using her time since to "give back" to her community.

Both women were charged in April following an investigation led by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) after conduct referrals.

Emily Barry, from the IOPC, said Doherty admitted supplying information to a man with known links to crime within a few months of her joining the force.

"Call handlers are privy to sensitive information and have access to confidential data on police systems," she added.

"It's incumbent on them not to inappropriately disclose information and to only access material for policing purposes."

Barry said the pair were likely to be barred from working in policing again following respective misconduct hearings.

title: He killed his 16-year-old ex-girlfriend 50 years ago. Florida just executed him.
description: The state executed Harold Gene Lucas by lethal injection for the 1976 murder of 16-year-old Jill Piper. Lucas was 24 at the time of the crime and was on death row for 50 years.
fullText:
Florida has executed a 74-year-old inmate who spent five decades on death row for shooting his teenage ex-girlfriend seven times even as she begged for her life. It's the first of eight scheduled executions in the U.S. in September, the most in a single month since 2010.

The state executed Harold Gene Lucas by lethal injection on Tuesday, Sept. 1, for the 1976 murder of 16-year-old Jill Piper in Bonita Springs, halfway between Fort Myers and Naples on Florida's Gulf Coast. Lucas was 24 at the time of murder.

Lucas, who was pronounced dead at 6:18 p.m. ET, became the 14th inmate executed in Florida this year, by far the most of any state. Florida governor Ron DeSantis continues an aggressive death penalty push as the end of his term approaches.

Lucas chose to accept his execution and waive further appeals after DeSantis signed his death warrant in July.

"I am 75 years old," Lucas recently told a court, though his 75th birthday would have been on Halloween. "I've been on death row for 50 years, and I have no desire to carry this any further . . . The sooner it's over, the better I'll enjoy it. I am tired."

Jill's brother, Buck Piper, told the Gulf Coast News that his father died waiting for justice but said that his 86-year-old mother would be front and center among the witnesses to the execution.

"They never got over the loss of their daughter," he told the station. "It's something that still weighs on her mind to this day."

Here's what you need to know about the execution, the crime, and why September is setting up to be the busiest single month for executions in 16 years.

On Aug. 14, 1976, Lucas had been drinking and doing hard drugs, got in a fight at a gas station, and told his friends he was going to "put that little (expletive) in a hole," according to court documents.

As Jill was returning home from a dance around midnight with two friends − 17-year-old Terri Rice and 19-year-old Richard Byrd Jr. − Lucas was lying in wait. Lucas fired four gunshots into Piper's back, and Rice and Byrd ran inside to call for help, court records say.

Though bleeding from the gunshot wounds, Piper was able to run inside. But Lucas followed, took her back outside and shot her three more times, including once in the back of the head, after she pleaded for her life. He then shot Byrd in the stomach and Rice in the hip. Both of them survived.

Lucas and Jill had dated for about four years when she broke up with him after an argument.

Part of the reason it has taken Florida so long to execute Lucas is because his death sentenced was vacated several times over the years, largely over procedural errors. Lucas has been re-sentenced to death altogether four times over the decades.

"It was an execution, pure and simple," prosecutor John Dommerich argued to jurors just before Lucas was sentenced to death for a fourth time in 1987, according to an archived story in the Naples Daily News, part of the USA TODAY Network. "He executed her when she begged for her life."

Lucas' attorneys had argued that he deserved mercy, saying he would never have killed Jill if he hadn't been drunk and high on hard drugs that night, including PCP.

At 16, Jill Piper was just getting started in life and was known for being just as sweet as she could be spunky, her younger brother, David Piper Jr., told the Naples Daily News on the 30th anniversary of her murder in 2006.

"She was tough," David Piper said at the time. "It was a scrappy little town here for many, many years, and she could take most of the guys, no problem ... But you can't fight bullets."

Even at 13, David Piper said he knew that Lucas was bad news and warned his sister to stay away from him. But, he said, Jill saw the good in everybody.

"She cared about people to the extreme," he said. "That's why she didn't get to live a long, fruitful life. Sometimes when people care to the extreme, they leave themselves wide open for dangerous situations to occur."

He told the newspaper that he tried not to think too much about his sister and didn't keep photos of her around.

"The only thing that will help is when Gene Lucas is put to death," he said.

Eight executions are scheduled to be carried out in five states this month. The executions include that of Christa Pike, the first woman set to be put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The last time at least eight executions were carried out in a single month in the U.S. was in 2010, according to a USA TODAY analysis of data tracked by the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center. That year, five states carried out nine executions in the month of May.

This month's spate of executions comes amid an overall uptick in the death penalty in the U.S. in the last two years. In 2025, 11 states executed 47 inmates, the most in any single year since 2009. So far this year, 24 inmates have been executed, with another 13 on the calendar through December, though more are expected to be added.

Experts attribute the increases to a friendlier death penalty climate under President Donald Trump and Florida's particularly aggressive execution push in the last two years.

Of the 71 executions carried out in the U.S. since 2025, Florida accounts for 32 of them. That's 45%, and that figure is increasing. Of this year's 24 executions, Florida has carried out 14. That's 58%.

Gov. Ron DeSantis, who decides which inmates are executed and when, has been drawing increasing criticism from death penalty opponents and observers who say the governor is being motivated by political ambition ahead of the 2028 presidential election and is "increasingly treating executions as routine instruments of political power," according to a recent statement from Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty.

DeSantis, whose second term as governor ends in January, has said he wants to give closure to families who have waited for justice sometimes longer than four decades.

Amanda Lee Myers is a senior crime reporter who covers cold case investigations and the death penalty for USA TODAY. Follow her on X at @amandaleeusat.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: He killed his 16-year-old ex-girlfriend 50 years ago. Florida just executed him.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Reacher' You Should Watch Next
description: More binge-worthy, often book-based crime dramas about heroic loners.
fullText:
After a couple of middling movies, Reacher, the series based on a series of more than 30 novels by Lee Childs, has been a breakout hit for Prime Video. It has been renewed through at least a fifth season, and there's a spin-off on the way—Neagley, starring Maria Sten. It's not hard to understand why audiences have connected to the story of an alarmingly large man who travels from town to town getting himself into trouble while helping others out of scrapes: The plotting is fun, the show doesn't take itself too seriously, and Alan Ritchson is a great physical match for the character while also selling the drifter-with-a-heart-of-gold vibe.

If you've finished your season four binge and need something new to watch, try one of the series below. Not all of them focus on outright loners like Reacher, and none of them are quite so large, but they all are more than capable of getting the job done solo.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings. Until...it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed and, unbeknownst to her, were also government operatives. Rescuing Rose puts Peter deep inside a web of conspiracy and official corruption. (This is why I never answer the phone.) Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There are like three dozen Alex Cross books (and counting), so there's plenty of material for this ongoing series (previously adapted into a series of films back in the '90s starring Morgan Freeman). Here, the D.C.-based homicide detective and forensic psychologist is played by Aldis Hodge as a guy every bit as committed to justice as Reacher. What sets Cross apart is the fact that he's also deeply committed to his family, which, rather than adding a charming bit of domesticity to the show, only ups the stakes as Cross's investigations frequently threaten to involve his kids. Stream Cross on Prime Video and Paramount+.

Tom Clancy's signature hero has been the star of books and films (starting with The Hunt for Red October) and has, at this point, outlived his creator by over a decade—despite the fact that he is never not in mortal danger. The latest incarnation, Prime Video's streaming series, stars John Krasinski as America's favorite CIA analyst, pulled from his desk job into the field after he discovers a pattern of suspicious bank transfers involving Islamic extremists. The show has ended, but the rather awkwardly titled Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan: Ghost War movie continues the series. Stream Tom Clancy's Jack Ryan on Prime Video.

The Queen Latifah-led Equalizer reboots the 1980s series (and sidesteps the Denzel Washington movies) by spinning the premise in a slightly different direction: Latifah plays single mom Robyn McCall, an impossibly skilled former CIA operative who puts her talents to work for those in need. It splits the difference between crime and spy drama, with some episodes involving close-to-home cases and others dealing with international espionage. While the original's vibe was more about the cops being handcuffed by things like "rules" and "giving perps their basic human dignity," this one is more about those who've been failed by systems that don't care about them—and who might benefit from the help of a woman who can beat just about anyone's ass. Stream The Equalizer on Paramount+ and Tubi.

Based on a popular novel series from Joe R. Lansdale, perhaps best known for his horror and western (and horror western) books, the show rather deftly blends genres—it's a heist show, a crime drama, and a buddy comedy set in the swamps around Baton Rouge in the 1980s. James Purefoy is Hap, a blue-collar ex-con (for avoiding the Vietnam draft) trying to live a quiet life, while the late Michael Kenneth Williams is Leonard, an openly gay vet with major anger management problems. One day, Hap's ex-wife shows up with an offer: the proceeds of a bank heist were lost, and if the two help her retrieve it, they'll get a cut, while she'll use the rest of money to fund her underground leftist group. Naturally, things get complicated rather quickly. Stream Hap and Leonard on AMC+.

Coming, as it does, from John le Carré, the wellspring of many modern spy sagas, it's probably no surprise that The Night Manager (from a 1993 novel, and not to be confused with The Night Agent up above) was successful—though it certainly doesn't hurt to have a cast led by Tom Hiddleston, Hugh Laurie, and Olivia Colman. Hiddleston is Jonathan Pine, working the night shift at a luxury hotel in Switzerland when he encounters an unexpected guest: arms dealer Richard Roper (Laurie). Former Army veteran Pine had previous dealings with Roper in Cairo, and the reluctant night manager is persuaded by Foreign Office head Angela Burr (Colman) to infiltrate the criminal's organization. Though he's been recruited by British intelligence, he remains an outsider, and perpetually on his own. The second season took about ten years to come about, but a third (and final?) should arrive a bit sooner. Stream The Night Manager on Prime Video.

Bosch is a more traditional crime drama, though one that wears its neo-noir aspirations on its sleeve. Titus Welliver is in the title role as LAPD detective Harry Bosch (star of the Michael Connelly novels), kicking off the series on trial for shooting a suspect in self-defense while investigating the murder of a 12-year-old. Like Reacher, Bosch draws on skills honed in the military and pursues criminals well beyond the limits, which is not always a great thing. Stream Bosch on Prime Video.

A usually engaging combination of smart plotting and lurid sex and violence, Banshee stars Antony Starr as Sheriff Lucas Hood...kinda. A man recently released from prison takes over that identity when the new sheriff in the small town of Banshee is killed. It's all part of a complicated plan to get back the $15 million in diamonds he lost when he went to jail. The new sheriff dispenses brutal justice without ever giving up his criminal ways, making him one of the greyest of TV's morally grey law-types. Stream Banshee on HBO Max.

Where Reacher is a loner from the jump, Luther's arc is one of one of increasing isolation, even as he cultivates an unsavory but steadfast ally. Idris Elba is DCI John Luther—a crime-solving genius whose preexisting inner demons are enabled by his work in investigating some of the darkest and most brutal crimes. Early on, he's unable to bring murderer Alice Morgan (Ruth Wilson) to justice, and the two become entangled in ways that benefit Luther's investigations while also threatening to bring him down entirely. The series proper is concluded, but there's a second spin-off film on the way, following The Fallen Sun. Stream Luther on Hulu.

Another hero of a long-running book series (this one from Jeffery Deaver), the tracker in question is Colter Shaw (Justin Hartley), a survivalist who travels the country (in his RV, naturally) selling his skills in finding missing persons. He's joined, remotely, by a team that includes a lawyer, handler, and the requisite computer guy—but they're all just the support team. At the end of the day, Shaw's the one who's gonna find your lost uncle. Stream Tracker on Paramount+.

title: North Carolina mountain town ‘whitewashing’ violence amid crime concerns, says pastor with former gang ties
description: Dr. Ronald Gates says Asheville, North Carolina, leaders ignored his gang prevention program for a decade before retaliatory shootings rattled the city.
fullText:
An Asheville pastor who says he had gang ties as a young man told Fox News Digital that city leaders ignored his decade-long push for a youth gang-prevention program before recent violence rattled the North Carolina tourist city.

Dr. Ronald Gates first brought the proposal to Asheville officials in 2016, urging them to invest in early intervention for children he believes could otherwise be pulled into dangerous groups and retaliatory violence.

The issue has taken on new urgency after a string of retaliatory shootings left two people dead and seven others wounded. City officials have stopped short of calling the violence gang-related, instead describing it as retaliation between groups of friends.

Mountain Getaway Rocked By 'Latest Chapter' Of Deadly Violence As Officials Avoid Gang Label In Tourist Town

Gates believes that distinction misses the larger problem.

"They did not want to actually acknowledge that it was gang activity," Gates told Fox News Digital. "They wanted to make sure that they tried to whitewash the narrative as they're saying that these are just retaliations between individuals."

Gates is the senior pastor of Greater Works Church of God in Christ. He also serves as a Buncombe County Sheriff's Office chaplain and describes himself as a community liaison who works with local law enforcement. His work in those roles has heightened his concern about young people drawn to violence by money, territory or a need for belonging.

His proposal centers on Gang Free, a Los Angeles-based program intended to help students in grades four through six understand how gangs recruit children and the consequences of becoming involved.

Raleigh Mayor Considers Youth Curfew Following Teen Takeover, Violent July 4Th Weekend

Gates learned about the program during a 2016 trip to California and returned determined to bring a similar effort to Asheville before youth violence became more entrenched.

"I said, 'Man, I've got to bring this back to Asheville, North Carolina,'" he recalled.

Over the past decade, Gates said, he has presented the proposal to mayors, city and county managers, police chiefs and sheriff's officials, urging them to give it a one-year trial.

He questioned why the city had not invested in the program, even temporarily, to see whether it could work locally.

The program, Gates explained, would teach children how gangs operate, including their signs and colors, and explain how older members can use younger people to move drugs, carry weapons or carry out other crimes.

Police Bigwig Accused Of Driving Son's Getaway Car In Gang Shooing Is Sorority Sisters With Mayor: Report

But education alone is not enough, he argued. A prevention model must also provide young people an alternative to the money and status that can make gangs attractive.

"These young men want to help provide for their single mom or their family," Gates said. "Any money that they can hustle up, they feel like they're doing something or doing their part."

Under his proposal, law enforcement officers, mentors and local business owners would work directly with children in their neighborhoods. Along with gang-prevention lessons, the program would provide educational help, mentorship and exposure to entrepreneurship.

Local businesses could show students how they operate and offer a path to earning money legally, Gates said, while the city could help fund stipends or similar opportunities.

Chicago Mayor Warns Of 'Teen Trend' After Takeover Chaos, Violence Concerns Grow

"Now they're learning how to make honest money, business money, capital, instead of putting their life on the line," he said.

Gates also has personal reason to believe early intervention can matter.

Growing up in Grand Rapids, Michigan, Gates had gang ties and was loosely associated with the Vice Lords. He credited his father, older brother and sports with keeping him from becoming more deeply involved.

"I thank God that someone intervened," Gates said.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

That experience shaped his belief that prevention has to begin before children become immersed in street life. Young people without steady father figures or mentors can look to older gang members for guidance and protection, he said, creating an opening for those figures to pressure them into dangerous acts while avoiding the harshest consequences themselves.

"If they would have had the opportunity, a different path, a different choice … could they still be here today?" Gates said, referring to young people caught up in the recent violence.

Gates recalled being told in 2016 that Asheville did not have the kind of gang activity that would warrant the program. He warned at the time that city leaders needed to get ahead of the problem rather than wait for violence to escalate.

"I said, 'Give it two years,'" Gates said. "Two years to the year."

State data shows Asheville reported 42% more violent crimes in 2024 than in 2016, even as its overall crime index fell 8%. The increase was driven largely by aggravated assaults, which rose from 335 to 558, while reported robberies declined. Violent crime peaked in 2022 and fell for two consecutive years, though the 2024 total remained above the city's 2016 level.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Fox News Digital has contacted Asheville officials for comment on Gates' claim that he repeatedly presented the prevention program to city leaders beginning in 2016, whether the city reviewed it and why it was not adopted.

Gates stressed that he was not arguing every violent dispute in Asheville is gang-related. But he said the city should not wait for a formal gang label before acting when young people are caught in cycles of retaliation.

"You have personal disputes," Gates said. "But then the thrust behind it, the motivation behind it is because, 'Look here, you spilled some blood. I'm going to spill some blood also.' And that's what it has come to."

For city leaders, the question is not just how a crime is labeled, Gates argued, but whether young people have enough opportunities to avoid the path that can lead to prison or death.

That means practical support long before a shooting, arrest or funeral.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"The prevention, it works if you put it out there," he said.

His message to anyone considering retaliation is simple: Speak with an older relative, a business owner or another trusted adult before making a choice that could change or end a life.

"Is it even worth retaliating?" Gates said. "Is it worth losing my life or going to prison for the rest of my life?"

"Let's use common sense," he added. "Count up the real costs."

title: Autopsy shows Tennessee National Guard fatally shot 20-year-old armed man in the back
description: Tennessee National Guard members assigned to a federal anti-crime task force in Memphis fatally shot an armed 20-year-old man in the back in July, an autopsy report obtained by The Associated Press sh...
fullText:
Tennessee National Guard members assigned to a federal anti-crime task force in Memphis fatally shot an armed 20-year-old man in the back in July, an autopsy report obtained by The Associated Press shows, contradicting police accounts that the man was facing the troops when they fired.

Authorities have said Tyrin Johnson turned toward guard members with a gun while running from them in the early morning hours after the Fourth of July holiday when he was fatally shot in the chest.

But according to an autopsy report shared Thursday by Johnson's family, a single bullet went in the right side of his back and exited through his upper right chest. The autopsy findings, reported earlier by The Commercial Appeal newspaper, were prepared by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center Office of the Medical Examiner, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The guard members were assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force, created by President Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democratic-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

Johnson's grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said guard members had no justification to shoot his grandson in the back.

"If he ain't caused you no threat, you know what I'm saying, you have no reason to be killing," said the former correctional officer with the Davidson County Sheriff's Office in Nashville.

Officers responded to a call of shots fired a few blocks from Beale Street and saw a person armed with a gun leaving, said Memphis police. Two Guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who "rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them," according to a Tennessee National Guard report obtained by the Associated Press. Both troops fired their service weapons, M17 handguns, and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the guard report said.

The bullet had a slightly upward trajectory through Tyrin Johnson's body, the autopsy report said. That would be consistent with him running away from the shooter, said Dr. Steven White, a certified forensic pathologist who did not do Johnson's autopsy but reviewed the report for the AP.

The report said there was no soot, gunpowder stippling or muzzle imprint around the wound, which White said indicated Johnson was likely shot from more than 3 feet away.

"Be transparent – you shot him in the back," Evaniel Johnson added. "I just want to make sure somebody be responsible for what happened. Some accountability. They ain't never going to bring my grandson back."

In the autopsy report, an "investigative narrative" based on an account from an agent with the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation also stated Tyrin Johnson was turning toward law enforcement with a gun.

"The unknown male grabbed at his waistband," the report stated. "Law enforcement officers saw the unknown male draw a firearm. Law enforcement officers then shot at the unknown male, striking him once in the chest."

Andre Wharton, an attorney representing Johnson's family, told the AP that the narrative presented by law enforcement does not match the autopsy findings of a single bullet wound in the back.

"I just see some kind of blatant inconsistency there, in terms of what law enforcement reports," Wharton said. "The versions don't seem to match."

The manner of death is listed as "homicide," which typically is used when a death is caused by the actions of another person but often doesn't factor in intent or carry any legal weight. To date, no criminal charges have been filed.

TBI said the investigation is "open and ongoing" and directed AP to the medical examiner's office when asked to confirm the autopsy findings. The AP has a pending request for a copy for Johnson's autopsy from the Shelby County Medical Examiner's office.

Johnson was carrying a "handgun magazine with rounds," according to the autopsy report. Wharton said it was not illegal for Johnson to be carrying the ammunition in Tennessee.

Johnson's family has asked authorities to show them surveillance video or other evidence he was pointing a weapon at guard members. The family has still not been shown any video of the moments leading up to the shooting, Evaniel Johnson said.

Trump's decision to send Tennessee National Guard troops to Memphis to combat crime was met with a mixed response from residents and was the subject of a lawsuit, though it did not result in widespread protests.

title: Federal judge says Trump discussing payoff to Stormy Daniels isn’t an official presidential action
description: A federal judge again denied President Donald Trump’s legal effort to get his New York state criminal hush money case moved to federal court, a move that could have made it easier to reverse his convi...
fullText:
A federal judge again denied President Donald Trump's legal effort to get his New York state criminal hush money case moved to federal court, a move that could have made it easier to reverse his conviction.

District Judge Alvin Hellerstein said in a ruling Friday that Trump's cited grounds were "neither new nor legally sufficient."

Hellerstein has previously denied Trump's request to move the case, but a federal appellate court ruled last fall that the district court judge must reconsider in light of the landmark presidential immunity ruling in July 2024 from the US Supreme Court.

The judge heard arguments from lawyers for Trump and prosecutors from the Manhattan District Attorney's office at a hearing in February but did not issue a ruling until now. Friday, Hellerstein maintained his position that Trump's acts as charged in the state's case against him were private and unrelated to his federal office.

"The People's prosecution arises from President Trump's private conduct surrounding the reimbursement of hush money payments to an adult film star," Hellerstein wrote Friday. "That conduct, and the challenged evidence, bears no substantive relation to his position in federal office. To consider these facts to be 'relating to' a federal office would give the words a definition that is 'so broad that it is meaningless.'"

Trump immediately appealed Friday's ruling.

"The Supreme Court's historic decision on Immunity, the Federal and New York State Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed," a spokesman for Trump's legal team said in a statement.

Lawyers for Trump have appealed his 2024 criminal conviction on 34 counts of falsifying business records tied to hush money payments to adult film star Stormy Daniels during the 2016 presidential election. Their separate efforts to get the case moved to federal court started before the state trial, so a federal judge could interpret federal preemption and presidential immunity. The federal track would also offer a faster route for his appeal to get to the Supreme Court.

Despite the guilty finding, Trump was sentenced to unconditional discharge, meaning he faced no penalties and the conviction was essentially in name only. It did, however, make Trump the first president convicted of a felony.

Months after his conviction, his lawyers tried again in the wake of the immunity decision that said presidents are protected from criminal prosecution for official acts and barred prosecutors from attempting to enter evidence involving official acts, even if they were pursuing alleged crimes involving that president's private conduct.

Trump's defense team has long argued Trump can't be prosecuted in connection to the hush money scheme because he's protected by presidential immunity – he reimbursed his former personal attorney Michael Cohen while in office for a cover up scheme Cohen orchestrated during the 2016 election.

In his latest ruling, the judge wrote, "There is no way that discussions regarding hush money payments to cover up the President's relations with Stormy Daniels could be an official act. An affair, or a cover-up of an affair, is not within the "'outer perimeter' of the President's official responsibilities."

For Trump, the debate is whether Manhattan prosecutors improperly introduced evidence involving White House staffers' actions at the hush money trial that they allege was Trump's crimes as an individual separate from his capacity as president.

Hellerstein disagreed: "A president's assistant can work on unofficial, personal matters for the president."

Last November, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals kicked the case back to Hellerstein and said the district court must reconsider but didn't weigh in on whether the SCOTUS decision should tip the scales for Trump.

Trump's lawyers also waited about two months to file that renewed request in federal court, first asking the state court Judge Juan Merchan to dismiss the conviction. Merchan denied the motion and Trump's appeal of his conviction is still moving through state appellate channels.

In February, Hellerstein called it a strategic decision to petition Merchan before the federal court. "You made a choice. You sought two bites at the apple," he said, signaling Friday's ruling back then.

In his order Friday, Hellerstein said Trump waited too long to file the renewed request for removal in federal court. "Trump's delay in filing for removal constitutes a "quintessential strategic decision," and the "fact that he later came to view that decision as a poor one is not sufficient, by itself, to establish cause."

The state appeal is also ongoing and could advance to the New York's Court of Appeals and potentially reach the US Supreme Court if Trump is unsuccessful at the lower appellate levels.

This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Dutch court sentences man to life over Rwanda genocide
description: The court in The Hague convicted the 66-year-old of war crimes and the crime of genocide.
fullText:
A court in the Netherlands has sentenced a Dutch-Rwandan man to life for his involvement in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

The 66-year-old, named only as Eugene N, was accused, among other things, of throwing a hand grenade into a crowd of Tutsis who were seeking shelter in a stadium. He was convicted of war crimes and the crime of genocide, having acted with "genocidal intent", the judge said.

Rwanda had sought his extradition in 2014 but the authorities in the Netherlands then launched their own investigation into N, who had become a Dutch citizen.

In 100 days in April 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed by Hutu extremists.

The court in The Hague heard N held an authoritative position in the community at the time of the massacre, overseeing around 1,000 people in Mbazi in southern Rwanda.

"The suspect was a man who was held in high regard and must have been aware of his role and the influence he had as a local administrator," the court explained, adding that he "committed multiple severe crimes".

At a football stadium, he instructed Hutus not to let any of the Tutsis escape. Trapped inside, they were pelted with stones, shot at and had hand grenades thrown at them.

Any who had survived, were killed with clubs and machetes, the court said.

Prior to the stadium massacre, N had watched on as people looted houses and set them on fire.

"Only a lifelong prison sentence does justice to the immense suffering that has been inflicted on the victims and the bereaved families," the court said.

As part of the Dutch investigation opened in 2020, more than 30 witnesses were interviewed. N was subsequently arrested in 2024.

N denied all the charges, the AFP news agency reports, alleging that he was a victim who had lost family in "those horrific events".

"The case has torn his scars open again. He is a broken man," his lawyers are quoted as saying by AFP. They had moved to seek acquittals on all accounts. N was acquitted of the incitement to genocide.

His defence team said they will "almost certainly appeal the charges", according to local news agency ANP.

title: Ex-Raiders RB Faces Criminal Charges as Potential NFL Suspension Looms
description: Former Las Vegas Raiders running back Josh Jacobs has been formally charged after an alleged domestic violence incident. The post Ex-Raiders RB Faces Criminal Charges as Potential NFL Suspension Looms appeared first on HEAVY.
fullText:
Former Las Vegas Raiders running back Josh Jacobs has been formally charged after an alleged domestic violence incident at his home in May.

Jacobs was initially accused of grabbing the arm of a woman identified as his girlfriend during a struggle in their home. He was charged on Thursday by prosecutors in Wisconsin, facing two misdemeanor charges related to the incident.

As ESPN reported, Jacobs was charged with misdemeanor battery and misdemeanor criminal damage to property.

"Our office sought to ensure a fair and complete review of available evidence, some of which only recently became available to our office due to significant, ongoing forensic efforts by law enforcement," Brown County District Attorney David L. Lasee said in a statement. "A criminal complaint is nothing more than a written, formal accusation against a defendant alleging the commission of criminal offenses and does not raise any inference of guilt. Mr. Jacobs is presumed innocent of these charges. As this is an ongoing criminal case, and out of respect for the rights of all parties, our office will not have further comment on the matter at this time."

Jacobs could risk nine months in prison and a fine of up to $10,000 for each charge if convicted.

The running back's lawyers released a statement noting that police did not formally charge him with domestic violence.

"The Brown County District Attorney has reviewed evidence and elected to file misdemeanor charges against Josh that do not include domestic violence," noted the lawyers, David Z. Chesnoff, Richard A. Schonfeld and Clarence F. Duchac III. "The allegations will be addressed in court, and not in the media. Mr. Jacobs respects the District Attorney's office and the process it followed."

Jacobs started his NFL career with the Raiders in 2019 and had success as the team's running back, leading the NFL in 2022 with 1,653 rushing yards. He joined the Packers in 2024.

Jacobs is set to make a court appearance on Nov. 17.

As ESPN noted, the league is investigating the allegations and could suspend Jacobs either to start the season or once his court case has concluded. The league has wide latitude to issue punishment in cases of alleged domestic violence, even if charges are ultimately dropped.

The Packers said they would continue to cooperate with the NFL during the investigation, but would not comment further on the charges.

title: Uefa preparing criminal legal action against Infantino
description: Uefa is pursuing criminal proceedings against Fifa president Gianni Infantino over the scrapped plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup.
fullText:
Uefa is preparing criminal legal proceedings against Fifa president Gianni Infantino over the now scrapped plan to sell off stakes in the World Cup and its other competitions to private investors.

Documents seen by BBC Sport show an application has been made by European football's governing body requesting access to evidence and documents for use in proceedings in Switzerland against the embattled president himself, who Uefa accuses of "criminal mismanagement".

Uefa also says it is considering pursuing criminal action against other Fifa officials.

Shortly after this summer's World Cup, Infantino proposed creating a new company, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would have sold off stakes in Fifa's football competitions to private investors.

The plan was scrapped after widespread backlash.

In the application for evidence, Uefa said: "In truth, it was a vehicle for Infantino and that small circle to acquire a permanent stake in and otherwise profit from Fifa's most valuable assets to the detriment of Fifa, its members, and other parties within the football family," Uefa's application says.

"Infantino pushed the plan through internal Fifa approval only days earlier at a hastily convened meeting where a limited number of Fifa's management officials and employees - some of whom had never heard of the plan - were given mere hours to sign off on an unprecedented multi-billion dollar scheme."

Key figures at Uefa and in European football met today in Monaco ahead of the Champions League draw, where Infantino's status was one item on the agenda.

A statement sent to the media by Uefa said: "Those present unanimously mandated the Uefa president and administration to pursue every available institutional, political and legal avenue necessary to secure fundamental reform, restore proper limits on presidential authority and ensure that Fifa is once again governed as an institution – not around one individual."

BBC Sport has approached Infantino and Fifa for comment.

Uefa also claims that the valuation of the stakes to be sold were not independently verified and would have been offered too cheaply, calling the proposed sale "a fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit".

The application adds: "Under the terms Infantino announced, those investors stood to acquire a permanent financial interest in Fifa's commercial arm for $4.2bn, implying an absurdly low enterprise value of only approximately $20bn, a figure that was neither the product of an open, competitive auction, nor tested by any independent valuer."

In the application, Uefa is applying to a court in Florida to attempt to access files held by two Fifa businesses - Fifa Americas and FWC2026 - to be used to pursue the criminal charges in Switzerland at a later stage.

The two businesses are based in Florida.

Uefa claims that its 55 member nations would have potentially been harmed by the sell-off plan, and that it may pursue criminal proceedings against other Fifa officials as well as Infantino.

"Uefa and other interested parties are preparing to bring criminal claims in Switzerland against Infantino and possibly other Fifa officials and advisors for criminal mismanagement," the application states.

"The secretive structuring, valuation, financing, and marketing inflicted direct and concrete injury on Fifa's reputation, governance authority, and commercial relationships to the detriment of Fifa as well as its 211 members, including Uefa's 55 member associations."

Uefa insists that the plan was concocted without the knowledge of them or other key stakeholders in football, and that it had been long in development.

The applications says: "On July 28, 2026, without consulting the Fifa Council, Uefa, or any of the other confederations, or any of the 211 Fifa member associations, Infantino, purportedly acting on behalf of Fifa, publicly announced a plan to place the commercial rights to the men's and women's World Cups and the Club World Cup into a new subsidiary: Fifa Forward Enterprise.

"That announcement by Infantino was the public unveiling of a plan that he and a small circle of co-conspirators had conceived and reportedly been developing in secret for more than a year."

Uefa states in the document that there has been "an enduring history of corruption among Fifa officials" and claims that world football's governing body only relents on its plans when pressure comes from outside the sport.

"Fifa's extraordinary power over world football has operated largely without meaningful internal constraint, with accountability coming principally through external forces, including political pressure, public scrutiny, and intervention through international criminal law enforcement," the application adds.

Fifa's headquarters are in the Swiss city of Zurich, and Uefa says that its plan to eventually pursue criminal charges against Infantino is backed up by Swiss law.

"Swiss counsel has confirmed [...] that the proceeding is within reasonable contemplation for purposes of Swiss law and that Uefa has standing, as a complainant, to file a criminal complaint for criminal mismanagement against Infantino and potentially other Fifa officials as may be warranted."

It has been reported that a separate filing has been lodged to a court in New York, where Uefa are seeking documentation from Thrive Capital, the business proposed to take up an interest in FFE which was founded by Josh Kushner, the brother of US president Donald Trump's son-in-law.

Reports indicate there is a third application in Colorado, relating to former Formula 1 chief Greg Maffei, who is referred to in the court filings as a "key commercial adviser" on the proposed FFE transaction.

BBC Sport has also approached Uefa for comment.

Uefa to push to remove Infantino after dropping boycott

Infantino offered Fifa's 211 member associations $40m (£30m) if they backed the proposal for private investment in its tournaments via FFE, including the men's and women's World Cups.

The Swiss has faced calls to step down after he scrapped the controversial plan earlier this month.

Uefa has led the backlash to the proposal, stating it had lost confidence in Infantino, and with its members voting to boycott World Cups unless the FFE plan was scrapped.

Infantino, who is seeking a fourth a term as Fifa president in March, was accused of breaking trust "through deception" in an open letter issued by Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation.

The football associations of all the home nations have withdrawn support for Infantino, but he retains the support of South American governing body Conmebol and Caf, the African governing body, while some nations have broken ranks from their confederations to come out in support of the Fifa president.

title: Trump criticism leads to rare criminal charges for Air Force officer who called for impeachment
description: A US airman who was arrested twice, once on the steps of the US Capitol while calling for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, was officially criminally charged Monday for his comments, accordin...
fullText:
A US airman who was arrested twice, once on the steps of the US Capitol while calling for the impeachment of President Donald Trump, was officially criminally charged Monday for his comments, according to a charging document his attorney shared with CNN.

Maj. Jason Watson faces the following charges under the Uniform Code of Military Justice, according to the document: three violations of Article 88 for alleged "contemptuous" remarks about Trump, five violations of Article 92 for allegedly disobeying orders and two violations of Article 133 for alleged conduct unbecoming an officer.

An Air Force spokesperson confirmed the charges on Tuesday.

"Maj. Watson will continue to be held in pre-trial confinement," the spokesperson said. "Airmen are afforded the right to due process, and considered innocent until proven guilty, in accordance with the Uniform Code of Military Justice."

The rare Article 88 charges are connected to the Air Force officer's June interview with the Defenders of our Republic Substack newsletter, his July 1 protest in uniform at the US Capitol, and an August 17 CNN interview.

It can be considered a violation of the Uniform Code of Military Justice to participate in uniform in any overtly partisan activity, such as a political protest, or to use "contemptuous words" against the president and other high-ranking civilian officials. Many low-level offenses of these rules are resolved informally, but Watson's violations were unusually high-profile.

Watson was first arrested in July while protesting in uniform at the US Capitol, and he was then arrested again last week just days after criticizing Trump again during a CNN interview. One of his attorneys, Chris Mutimer, told CNN that his client was ordered to remain in "pre-trial confinement" — an action analogous to a denial of bond in civilian court — pending legal action against him.

"Not only is (Trump) a failure as president, he is flagrantly violating the Constitution, breaking the law, engaged in rampant corruption, and is killing Americans," Watson told CNN's Erin Burnett during the interview. "And that is unacceptable to me."

In July, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said in a social media post that he expected all airmen to "comply with all laws and policies government personal conduct, political participation, and the wear of the uniform."

"Americans place their trust in us," Meink said. "We cannot, and will not, compromise the trust of the nation."

The disobeying orders charges against Watson allege that he violated Defense Department regulations barring troops from speaking out in favor of partisan causes; "wrongfully" wore his uniform at a Capitol press conference; broke leave regulations by traveling to Washington, DC; and refused to wear his uniform to work the morning after his CNN interview.

Air Force prosecutors also alleged that Watson's Capitol protest and CNN interview constituted "conduct unbecoming an officer."

Mutimer, Watson's attorney, told CNN's Erin Burnett on "OutFront" that he spoke with his client Monday and "he is basically in solitary confinement for his safety."

Mutimer said, "He truly believes in everything about our constitution and what it represents, and the oath that he swore, and he stands by the fact that he did this so others wouldn't have to, and to share that to anyone who's scared and feels alone."

The founder of the organization that organized the protest in July, Jessica Denson of the Removal Coalition, told CNN at the time that Watson was aware of the risks of what he was doing and had reached out to them via email.

"We started having conversations and took this desire that he had to come out very seriously and thought about the best way to make his sacrifice worth it," Denson said.

Military courts-martial leading to "contempt of officials" charges are rare — a CNN review only identified two such convictions that have occurred since the modern Uniform Code of Military Justice was enacted in 1951.

In 1965, an Army lieutenant was convicted of the charge after he participated in an off-base protest against the Vietnam War in El Paso, Texas. Lt. Henry Howe was sentenced to a dismissal from the service — the equivalent of a dishonorable discharge for an officer — and a year in the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas. Defense Secretary Robert McNamara ultimately granted parole to Howe, ending his sentence early.

The most recent Article 88 conviction came in 2021, when former Marine Corps Lt. Col. Stuart Scheller pleaded guilty to contempt of officials and other charges linked to a series of social media videos he published criticizing the Biden administration's handling of the US military's withdrawal from Afghanistan. Scheller, who was confined to the brig for a period of time before his trial, was sentenced to a $5,000 pay forfeiture and resigned from the Marine Corps sans-pension as part of a plea agreement.

The Trump administration has since appointed Scheller to serve as a senior adviser to the Pentagon's undersecretary for personnel and readiness.

Frank Rosenblatt, a retired Army judge advocate and associate law professor at Mississippi Christian University, said to CNN that the standard for "contemptuous" words is "less than precise" in guidance provided to military judges and panel members (similar to jurors).

Rosenblatt said that "contemptuous" remarks under Article 88 must be "insulting, rude, and disdainful conduct, or otherwise disrespectfully attributing to another a quality of meanness, disreputableness, or worthlessness."

He suggested that a pretrial hearing known as an Article 32 proceeding may be required to assess whether Watson's remarks instead "are true or are fair criticisms" of the president.

It remains to be seen whether Watson's case will be referred to trial, and whether that trial will be considered a special or general court-martial. Special courts-martial are roughly equivalent to misdemeanor trials, and general courts-martial are analogous to felony trials and can hand down more severe sentences.

This story has been updated with additional details.

CNN's Piper Hudspeth Blackburn, Carmen Conte Widman and Francesca Giuliani Hoffman contributed to this report.
